nameStory: The 'Osage' part honors the Osage Nation, who prized this tree's incredibly strong, flexible wood for making the finest bows. The 'orange' part comes from the bumpy, round fruit that looks like a bright green-yellow citrus fruit, though it's not related to oranges at all!
description: Osage-orange is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree that grows 30-50 feet tall, originally from the south-central United States but planted throughout New England. It's famous for its bizarre, brain-like fruits that are bright yellow-green and roughly the size of a softball. The tree has a rounded crown and belongs to the mulberry family, not the citrus family despite its name.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Unmistakable bumpy, wrinkled fruits about 4-6 inches across that look like green brains or warty oranges. When cut, they ooze sticky white latex that will get all over your hands - definitely wear gloves!

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, oval leaves 3-5 inches long with smooth edges and a pointed tip. They're arranged alternately on the branch and turn bright yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Orange-brown bark that becomes deeply furrowed with age, creating distinctive ridges and valleys you can run your fingers along.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows in a somewhat irregular, spreading shape with thorny branches when young. May appear more shrub-like if repeatedly cut back.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Sharp thorns up to an inch long grow along the branches - watch out when examining closely! These are most prominent on younger growth.

habitat: In New England, you'll typically find Osage-orange around old farmsteads, along roadsides, and in abandoned fields where it was originally planted as living fence posts. It thrives in full sun and tolerates poor, dry soils better than most trees. Look for it in rural areas and older suburban neighborhoods rather than deep forests.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous greenish flowers appear in late spring after the leaves emerge. The glossy new leaves are bright green and very noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Full leafed out with dense, dark green foliage. Young fruits begin developing and growing larger through the summer months.
seasonality.fall: The bizarre softball-sized fruits ripen to bright yellow-green and fall to the ground, while leaves turn brilliant yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny branches reveal the orange-brown furrowed bark pattern. Old fruits may persist on the ground, turning brown and wrinkled.

funFact: Scientists think these weird fruits evolved to be eaten by giant ground sloths and mastodons - but since those animals went extinct 10,000 years ago, the fruits just fall and rot because almost nothing alive today has a mouth big enough to eat them!
confusionNotes: The fruit is so distinctive that mature trees are unmistakable, but young trees without fruit might be confused with other thorny trees like honey locust. However, honey locust has compound leaves with many small leaflets, while Osage-orange has simple, single leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Osage-orange is completely unrelated to citrus oranges - it's actually in the mulberry family. The fruits are technically edible but taste terrible and have a texture like cardboard, though some people still use them as natural insect repellents in basements.
compareHints: Osage-orange is the only member of its genus (Maclura) in New England, making it unique in the region. Its closest relatives in the mulberry family are actual mulberries, but those have much smaller, blackberry-like clustered fruits and lack the thorns. The massive, brain-textured fruits make Osage-orange impossible to confuse with anything else in New England.
